- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`; shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- In your reply, a thread's first mention is its `link` verbatim. No `link`: `[title](t3-thread://v1/<exact id>)`. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A secret: call `request_secret` yourself. Pass its `secretRef` to a T3 tool, or use `delivery: "file"` for a shell command. Never ask in chat or invent one. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.

### Visuals and preview

- Show trends, comparisons, and flows as a chart or diagram, even unasked, and any visual the user asks for here: pass its HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. If the visual is a file, pass that file's HTML. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Tools a web page exposes give data only. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` to verify or show your own edit, even a frontend edit or an open tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Use them only when the current request asks for browser work or names a page or tab. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.


### Background work you wait on

To wait for a background command or Monitor you started (tests, a build), call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID before you end your turn. Do not mark work you leave running, or PRs. T3 MCP tools are deferred: load one with ToolSearch before you call it.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text:
CI is green on the fix: https://github.com/chrisdoc/pi-pii-redact/pull/17 is ready to merge. All 5 checks passed on `ca0e6ea`, and CodeRabbit's review had no comments to act on. Once it's merged, `main` should pass again.

**What was failing:** the model library (`@desert-ant-labs/redact` 4.2.1) sometimes crashes with a segmentation fault as the process exits. The test from #15 started a child process and required it to exit cleanly, so CI failed whenever the child crashed. This only happens on CI's x64 runners. In the CI run where I repeated it 30 times, 6 crashed on Node 22 and none on Node 24 (Node 24 had also failed on `main` before). Every crash came after the test's checks had already run and the model had been released, so the code from #15 isn't at fault.

**The fix (test-only, so no changeset):** the tests now require the child to reach a `disposed` marker printed after the model is released, instead of a clean exit code. They still check stderr as before. If the child dies earlier, the failure message shows the signal and the child's stderr. The PR is squashable: one temporary commit added and then removed the repeat test.

**Still open:** the crash itself isn't fixed and probably affects real use. Pi releases the model when a session ends and then exits, so it may occasionally segfault on quit on x64 Linux. It's worth reporting to the `@desert-ant-labs` maintainers, and I can draft that report if you want.

I've stopped watching the PR.

# Masker Mini (v3)

**Masker-mini** is the on-device sibling of
[**masker**](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker). It is a 6-layer
distilled PII detector for **23 European languages** that fits in **18 MB**
(4-bit Core ML) or **22 MB** (4-bit ONNX).

It runs fully offline, so no PII leaves the device.

| artifact                            | format                    | size      | token agreement vs fp32 | strict F1 |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------- | --------- |
| `model.safetensors`                 | PyTorch fp16              | 71 MB     | —                       | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_fp16.onnx`              | ONNX fp16 (portable)      | 71 MB     | 100%                    | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_int4.onnx`              | ONNX 4-bit (ONNX Runtime) | **22 MB** | 99.95%                  | 0.975     |
| `coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` | Core ML 4-bit (Apple NE)  | **18 MB** | 99.93%                  | 0.974     |

Per-artifact columns are measured on a 2,000-document openpii validation sample.

### What's new in v3

- **Much better on real text.** On out-of-distribution person names (real court
  judgments and Dutch news), names F1 goes from **0.774 → 0.865**. Leak recall
  goes from 0.868 → 0.922. It beats `nationaldesignstudio/rampart` (0.690) and
  `desert-ant-labs/redact` (0.626) on every metric we measure.
- **Far fewer false names in Dutch.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, the share of other named
  entities (companies, places) wrongly tagged as persons drops from **16.4% →
  7.0%**.
- **One change caused it: the student now starts from pretrained weights.** v2's
  student started from random weights, so everything it knew about language came
  from the distillation data. v3 starts from the bottom six layers of
  [Multilingual-MiniLM](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384),
  moved onto masker's 64K tokenizer. The teacher, the data and the recipe are
  otherwise identical to v2.
- **Drop-in replacement for v2.** The architecture, `config.json`, label map,
  tokenizer files (byte-identical), inputs and outputs are all the same. You only
  swap the weights. v2 is kept under the
  [`v2` tag](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini/tree/v2).

## Model type & training
## Usage

For a plain PyTorch / Transformers quick start, the snippet on the
[masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker) card runs unchanged. Just
point it at `divergentlabs/masker-mini`.

This repo exists mainly for the two on-device builds:

**ONNX Runtime** (portable for Android, iOS, web, server)

```python
import onnxruntime as ort, numpy as np
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

repo = "divergentlabs/masker-mini"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
sess = ort.InferenceSession(hf_hub_download(repo, "onnx/model_fp16.onnx"))
text = "Sanne de Groot woont in Utrecht."
feed = {k: v.astype(np.int64) for k, v in tok(text, return_tensors="np").items()}
logits = sess.run(None, feed)[0]        # [1, seq_len, 49] BIOES logits -> argmax + decode
```

For the smallest portable build, swap in `onnx/model_int4.onnx` (22 MB, 4-bit).
It has the same inputs and outputs and needs ONNX Runtime ≥ 1.18.

**Swift (iOS / macOS):** [**swift-masker**](https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker)
is a Swift package that wraps the Core ML build with tokenization, the
BIOES→span decode, the structured-PII rules layer, and reversible masking. It
bundles its own copy of the model. v3 uses the same tokenizer and interface as
v2, so the bundled model can be swapped without code changes.

```swift
// .package(url: "https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker.git", from: "0.1.0")
let masker = try await Masker()
let masked = try await masker.mask(userText)   // "[EMAIL_1] lives in [CITY_1]"
let final  = masker.unmask(reply, with: masked.session)
```

To use the **Core ML** model directly, add
`coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` to an Xcode target. Its inputs are
`input_ids`, `attention_mask` and `token_type_ids` (`Int32`, fixed length 256),
and its output is `logits` (`[1, 256, 49]`, fp16). Tokenize with this repo's
`spm.model` / `tokenizer.json`.

## Limitations & biases

- **Some Dutch over-redaction remains.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, 7.0% of the other
  named entities are still tagged as persons, against 2.7% for the teacher. Brand
  names built from a person's name are the typical case: "Albert Heijn" (a
  supermarket chain) is tagged as a person. For Dutch documents where
  over-redaction matters, use [masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker).
- **Dutch _tussenvoegsel_ surnames may be mistyped on short inputs.** v2 sometimes
  typed the surname of "Sanne de Groot" or "Pieter van den Berg" as
  `STREET_NAME` or `CITY`. We did not reproduce this with v3, but have not ruled
  it out. When it happens, the characters are still redacted; only the
  placeholder type is wrong.
- **This is a compressed model.** It trails the full-size masker (v2) by about
  0.9 points strict F1 in-distribution and by 7.3 points names F1 on real text. The
  loss lands almost entirely on `GIVEN_NAME` / `SURNAME`. Structured types (email,
  phone, IDs, cards, dates) stay ≥ 0.99.
- The out-of-distribution sets cover only English legal text and Dutch news.
  Measure on your own text, and design for residual leakage rather than assuming
  full coverage.

## Credits & attribution

Initialised from **Multilingual-MiniLM** and distilled from **masker**:

- **Student initialisation:** [`microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384)
  by Microsoft, **MIT License**. masker-mini v3 starts from its bottom six layers.
  MiniLM: Wang et al., 2020 ([arXiv:2002.10957](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10957)).

masker is itself a derivative of:

- **Backbone / tokenizer lineage:** [`microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base)
  by Microsoft, **MIT License**. masker-mini uses a pruned version of mDeBERTa's
  SentencePiece tokenizer. DeBERTaV3: He, Gao & Chen, 2021
  ([arXiv:2111.09543](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09543)).
- **Synthetic training data:** [`ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m)
  by **Ai4Privacy**, **CC-BY-4.0**.
- **Real-text training data** (person annotations, used for masker v2 and as
  distillation text):
  - [Universal NER](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BramVanroy/universal_ner):
    en_ewt, da_ddt, pt_bosque, sk_snk, sr_set, sv_talbanken. Mayhew et al., 2024.
    **CC-BY-SA-4.0**
  - GermEval 2014 (de) and AnCora (es), via the
    [OpenNER standardized](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bltlab/open-ner-standardized)
    collection. **CC-BY-4.0**
  - [SUC-X 3.0](https://huggingface.co/datasets/KBLab/sucx3_ner) (sv), **CC-BY-4.0**
  - [KPWr](https://huggingface.co/datasets/clarin-pl/kpwr-ner) (pl), **CC-BY-3.0**
  - [EstNER](https://huggingface.co/datasets/tartuNLP/EstNER) (et), **CC-BY-4.0**
  - [RONEC](https://huggingface.co/datasets/community-datasets/ronec) (ro), **MIT**
  - [hr500k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/classla/hr500k) (hr), **CC-BY-SA-4.0**
  - [Turku NER corpus](https://github.com/TurkuNLP/turku-ner-corpus) (fi),
    **CC-BY-SA-4.0**
  - [WikiNER-fr-gold](https://huggingface.co/datasets/danrun/WikiNER-fr-gold) (fr),
    **CC-BY-4.0**
- **Evaluation only:** [TAB](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ildpil/text-anonymization-benchmark)
  (MIT) and CoNLL-2002 Dutch (Tjong Kim Sang, 2002).

Please retain these credits in downstream use.

## License

Licensed under the **Apache License, Version 2.0**. See `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

The underlying components keep their own terms, listed in Credits above.

v2 (the [`v2` tag](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini/tree/v2)) is

[`v1` tag](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini/tree/v1)) were released
under the Offchain Studio Source License, Version 1.0, and remain under those terms.

---

# Masker Mini (v3)

**Masker-mini** is the on-device sibling of
[**masker**](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker). It is a 6-layer
distilled PII detector for **23 European languages** that fits in **18 MB**
(4-bit Core ML) or **22 MB** (4-bit ONNX).

It runs fully offline, so no PII leaves the device.

| artifact                            | format                    | size      | token agreement vs fp32 | strict F1 |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------- | --------- |
| `model.safetensors`                 | PyTorch fp16              | 71 MB     | —                       | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_fp16.onnx`              | ONNX fp16 (portable)      | 71 MB     | 100%                    | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_int4.onnx`              | ONNX 4-bit (ONNX Runtime) | **22 MB** | 99.95%                  | 0.975     |
| `coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` | Core ML 4-bit (Apple NE)  | **18 MB** | 99.93%                  | 0.974     |

Per-artifact columns are measured on a 2,000-document openpii validation sample.

### What's new in v3

- **Much better on real text.** On out-of-distribution person names (real court
  judgments and Dutch news), names F1 goes from **0.774 → 0.865**. Leak recall
  goes from 0.868 → 0.922. It beats `nationaldesignstudio/rampart` (0.690) and
  `desert-ant-labs/redact` (0.626) on every metric we measure.
- **Far fewer false names in Dutch.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, the share of other named
  entities (companies, places) wrongly tagged as persons drops from **16.4% →
  7.0%**.
- **One change caused it: the student now starts from pretrained weights.** v2's
  student started from random weights, so everything it knew about language came
  from the distillation data. v3 starts from the bottom six layers of
  [Multilingual-MiniLM](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384),
  moved onto masker's 64K tokenizer. The teacher, the data and the recipe are
  otherwise identical to v2.
- **Drop-in replacement for v2.** The architecture, `config.json`, label map,
  tokenizer files (byte-identical), inputs and outputs are all the same. You only
  swap the weights. v2 is kept under the
  [`v2` tag](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini/tree/v2).

## Model type & training
## Usage

For a plain PyTorch / Transformers quick start, the snippet on the
[masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker) card runs unchanged. Just
point it at `divergentlabs/masker-mini`.

This repo exists mainly for the two on-device builds:

**ONNX Runtime** (portable for Android, iOS, web, server)

```python
import onnxruntime as ort, numpy as np
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

repo = "divergentlabs/masker-mini"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
sess = ort.InferenceSession(hf_hub_download(repo, "onnx/model_fp16.onnx"))
text = "Sanne de Groot woont in Utrecht."
feed = {k: v.astype(np.int64) for k, v in tok(text, return_tensors="np").items()}
logits = sess.run(None, feed)[0]        # [1, seq_len, 49] BIOES logits -> argmax + decode
```

For the smallest portable build, swap in `onnx/model_int4.onnx` (22 MB, 4-bit).
It has the same inputs and outputs and needs ONNX Runtime ≥ 1.18.

**Swift (iOS / macOS):** [**swift-masker**](https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker)
is a Swift package that wraps the Core ML build with tokenization, the
BIOES→span decode, the structured-PII rules layer, and reversible masking. It
bundles its own copy of the model. v3 uses the same tokenizer and interface as
v2, so the bundled model can be swapped without code changes.

```swift
// .package(url: "https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker.git", from: "0.1.0")
let masker = try await Masker()
let masked = try await masker.mask(userText)   // "[EMAIL_1] lives in [CITY_1]"
let final  = masker.unmask(reply, with: masked.session)
```

To use the **Core ML** model directly, add
`coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` to an Xcode target. Its inputs are
`input_ids`, `attention_mask` and `token_type_ids` (`Int32`, fixed length 256),
and its output is `logits` (`[1, 256, 49]`, fp16). Tokenize with this repo's
`spm.model` / `tokenizer.json`.

## Limitations & biases

- **Some Dutch over-redaction remains.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, 7.0% of the other
  named entities are still tagged as persons, against 2.7% for the teacher. Brand
  names built from a person's name are the typical case: "Albert Heijn" (a
  supermarket chain) is tagged as a person. For Dutch documents where
  over-redaction matters, use [masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker).
- **Dutch _tussenvoegsel_ surnames may be mistyped on short inputs.** v2 sometimes
  typed the surname of "Sanne de Groot" or "Pieter van den Berg" as
  `STREET_NAME` or `CITY`. We did not reproduce this with v3, but have not ruled
  it out. When it happens, the characters are still redacted; only the
  placeholder type is wrong.
- **This is a compressed model.** It trails the full-size masker (v2) by about
  0.9 points strict F1 in-distribution and by 7.3 points names F1 on real text. The
  loss lands almost entirely on `GIVEN_NAME` / `SURNAME`. Structured types (email,
  phone, IDs, cards, dates) stay ≥ 0.99.
- The out-of-distribution sets cover only English legal text and Dutch news.
  Measure on your own text, and design for residual leakage rather than assuming
  full coverage.

## Credits & attribution

Initialised from **Multilingual-MiniLM** and distilled from **masker**:

- **Student initialisation:** [`microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384)
  by Microsoft, **MIT License**. masker-mini v3 starts from its bottom six layers.
  MiniLM: Wang et al., 2020 ([arXiv:2002.10957](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10957)).

masker is itself a derivative of:

- **Backbone / tokenizer lineage:** [`microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base)
  by Microsoft, **MIT License**. masker-mini uses a pruned version of mDeBERTa's
  SentencePiece tokenizer. DeBERTaV3: He, Gao & Chen, 2021
  ([arXiv:2111.09543](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09543)).
- **Synthetic training data:** [`ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m)
  by **Ai4Privacy**, **CC-BY-4.0**.
- **Real-text training data** (person annotations, used for masker v2 and as
  distillation text):
  - [Universal NER](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BramVanroy/universal_ner):
    en_ewt, da_ddt, pt_bosque, sk_snk, sr_set, sv_talbanken. Mayhew et al., 2024.
    **CC-BY-SA-4.0**
  - GermEval 2014 (de) and AnCora (es), via the
    [OpenNER standardized](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bltlab/open-ner-standardized)
    collection. **CC-BY-4.0**
  - [SUC-X 3.0](https://huggingface.co/datasets/KBLab/sucx3_ner) (sv), **CC-BY-4.0**
  - [KPWr](https://huggingface.co/datasets/clarin-pl/kpwr-ner) (pl), **CC-BY-3.0**
  - [EstNER](https://huggingface.co/datasets/tartuNLP/EstNER) (et), **CC-BY-4.0**

content.thinking:
Comparing label coverage, masker-mini supports only 12 entity types versus the current setup's 22, notably lacking SECONDARY_ADDRESS and STATE.

On the engineering side, there's no JS SDK for this model, so integrating it would require onnxruntime-node, a tokenizer setup, BIOES decoding with offsets, chunking for long sequences, and softmax-based confidence scoring -- transformers.js could potentially simplify this by handling tokenization and ONNX execution together. Size-wise, int4 at 22MB seems more practical for a Node CLI than fp16 at 71MB, especially since fp16 operations often upcast or run slowly on CPU while int4 MatMulNBits is CPU-optimized, so benchmarking both would be worthwhile before deciding.

I'm also wondering whether switching models would actually resolve the segfault -- it plausibly would, since it removes the native desert-ant core along with its license verification and telemetry calls. That raises a separate point worth checking: whether the current library phones home via something like DAL_LICENSE_ENDPOINT, since moving to an open Apache-2.0 model would also eliminate that network dependency.

Their benchmark claims against desert-ant-labs/redact are self-reported and unverified, though regex overlay hooks still exist. My instinct is to recommend a cautious spike behind a backend abstraction, testing int4 and fp16 variants against our e2e tiers rather than switching outright, since we'd lose some label coverage like DATE/AGE that the current model may support -- I should offer this assessment and ask if they want a prototype rather than just diving in.

content.text:
I think it's worth a trial, but I wouldn't switch straight over. Its main advantages: it would drop the closed native library that segfaults on exit, it's Apache-2.0, and it claims better name detection. The catch is that it covers about half the PII types we redact today, and we'd have to build the runtime pieces that `@desert-ant-labs/redact` currently gives us.

**What it improves**
- **It would drop the crash we just found.** The segfault, the use of koffi to call native code, and the license-verifier callback all come from `@desert-ant-labs`. The current core also has a license endpoint and telemetry hooks. masker-mini is Apache-2.0 open weights run through ONNX Runtime, with nothing calling home.
- **Names.** Their card claims a person-name F1 of 0.865 versus 0.626 for `desert-ant-labs/redact` on real text (English court judgments and Dutch news). The authors measured that themselves and nobody has verified it, but names are where false negatives hurt us most.
- **Languages and portability:** it covers 23 European languages, and the ONNX file runs on Node, the web and mobile.

**What we'd lose**
- **Label coverage.** It has 12 types: `GIVEN_NAME`, `SURNAME`, `STREET_NAME`, `BUILDING_NUMBER`, `CITY`, `ZIP_CODE`, `EMAIL`, `PHONE`, `CREDIT_CARD`, `GOVERNMENT_ID`, `DATE` and `AGE`. Our rules use 22. These would have no model behind them:
  - `SECONDARY_ADDRESS`, `STATE`, `BANK_ACCOUNT`, `ROUTING_NUMBER`, `URL`
  - `PASSPORT`, `DRIVERS_LICENSE`, `TAX_ID`, `SSN`, `IMEI`, `ORG`

  Only email, IP address and generic API keys have regex rules today, so most of these would need new regex rules or would simply stop being redacted. It also adds `DATE`, which could over-redact dates in timestamps, git logs and changelogs, which is a lot of what a coding agent reads. I'd ship `DATE` disabled by default.
- **We'd have to build what the current SDK does for us:**
  - `onnxruntime-node`, which is another native dependency, though a mainstream and well-maintained one.
  - A JavaScript tokenizer for its SentencePiece `tokenizer.json`.
  - Decoding its BIOES tags into character spans.
  - Softmax confidence scores for `minimumConfidence`.
  - Splitting inputs longer than 512 tokens into overlapping windows, since tool output is often long.

  `@huggingface/transformers` could handle the tokenizer and runtime, but its token-classification pipeline doesn't decode BIOES tags properly, so we'd write that part ourselves.

**fp16 vs int4:** I'd lean towards `model_int4.onnx` (22 MB, 99.95% agreement with full precision) rather than fp16 (71 MB). On CPU, ONNX Runtime has optimised kernels for the 4-bit format, while fp16 often gets converted back to fp32 and may not be faster. The int4 file is also about the size of today's model (24 MB cached). Their card shows the same 0.975 F1 for both.

**What I'd suggest:** a time-boxed trial behind a small backend interface in `RedactorService`, keeping the current model as the default. We'd run the existing e2e tiers against both backends, comparing what leaks, false positives on code and logs, latency and memory. If the trial wins, switching becomes a config change and we add regex rules for the lost types. If it loses, we've only spent the trial.

Should I scope and start that trial?

content.content:
# Masker (v2)

**masker** is a multilingual token classifier for personally identifiable
information (PII) in **23 European languages**. It is the neural half of a
two-part redaction system. This model tags _contextual_ PII: names, addresses,
ages and dates.

A separate, dependency-free rules layer handles _structured_ PII (IBANs, cards,
national IDs) with real checksum validation. Where both fire on the same span,
the checksum-validated rule wins. Everywhere else, the model decides. This
repository is the neural half and the **full-accuracy reference model** of the
family.

📱 Need something small enough to run on a phone or in a web browser? See
[**masker-mini**](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini), a 6-layer
[`microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base)
with **boundary-first BIOES supervision**. It was trained for 1 epoch on 1.44M
rows: name-form-augmented
[`ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m)
plus the real-text corpora. In the real text, person spans come from the gold
annotations (split into given name and surname by masker v1, or by rule), and the other
PII types are pseudo-labelled by masker v1.

The head predicts **12 entity types** (48 BIOES labels + `O`):

`GIVEN_NAME`, `SURNAME`, `CITY`, `STREET_NAME`, `BUILDING_NUMBER`, `ZIP_CODE`,
`PHONE`, `EMAIL`, `CREDIT_CARD`, `DATE`, `AGE`, `GOVERNMENT_ID`.

`GOVERNMENT_ID` covers passport, national-ID, SSN, tax and driver-license
numbers; the rules layer tells them apart by checksum and format. Other
structured types (IBAN, IP, URL, etc.) are owned entirely by the rules layer and
are not part of this head.

## Usage

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForTokenClassification
import torch

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("divergentlabs/masker")
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained("divergentlabs/masker").eval()

text = "Kundin Beatrix Möller, geb. 04.07.1979, Rosenweg 8, 50667 Köln."
enc = tok(text, return_tensors="pt", return_offsets_mapping=True)
offsets = enc.pop("offset_mapping")[0]
with torch.no_grad():
    labels = model(**enc).logits.argmax(-1)[0]
for (a, b), lab in zip(offsets.tolist(), labels.tolist()):
    if b > a and model.config.id2label[lab] != "O":
        print(text[a:b].strip(), "->", model.config.id2label[lab])
```

The raw output is per-token BIOES labels. The companion `mask` package turns
them into character spans and merges them with the rules layer. The tokenizer's
offsets include the leading space of word-initial pieces, so trim whitespace
from span edges.

I'm thinking through boundary-first BIOES supervision, where B/E mark span boundaries and interior tokens can be O, so decoding follows B to its matching E while skipping O tokens. The model seems weak on email spans specifically, which is fine since our regex overlay handles emails separately, and now I'm checking how it performs on phone number spans.

The phone number got missed entirely while the card was tagged as PHONE — structured types are clearly weak here, confirming the model is meant to lean on a rules layer rather than detect these itself. That means I'll need to build out that rules layer covering phone numbers, card numbers with Luhn validation, IBANs, and ID formats; I'm also curious about the "companion mask package" mentioned and want to check if there's a published JS or Python mask package under divergentlabs on PyPI or GitHub.

Found that the model uses "boundary-first BIOES" tagging (decode from begin to end tag, not every token) plus a separate rules layer for structured PII with checksums—explaining the missed phone number and mislabeled card. I'll check if that rules layer and decoder are available in an existing package.

I'm also noting onnxruntime-node's install footprint (roughly 25-46MB per platform plus a ~22MB model) and confirming its postinstall script doesn't cause issues outside of protobufjs skipping install scripts.

My plan for the trial scope: build a `NerBackend` interface with a `desertAntBackend` wrapping the existing logic and a new `maskerMiniBackend` using onnxruntime-node plus HF tokenizers, downloading the model from HF into a cache directory pinned to a commit SHA, defaulting to int4 with an fp16 option, and handling offset-aware tokenization, chunking with overlap, BIOES decoding, softmax confidence, and deduplication. I also need to add backend selection to the config.

For the backend selection, I'll keep it constructor/env-var only for the trial (via PI_PII_REDACT_BACKEND) rather than persisting it in pii-config, to limit surface area. I'm mapping masker labels to existing rule labels like GIVEN_NAME, SURNAME, STREET_NAME, EMAIL, PHONE, CREDIT_CARD, etc., with DATE and AGE as new possible additions for the trial only, and any unsupported nativeLabels simply producing no output.

The test answered the main feasibility questions, so I'll wait for the scoper's report on the redactor code before writing the plan.

Feasibility results so far:
- **Runtime:** `onnxruntime-node` 1.31.1 and `@huggingface/tokenizers` 0.2.0 load masker-mini under Node 24. On three short examples, int4 took about 17–26 ms and fp16 about 27–41 ms on this ARM machine.
- **Detection:** names, streets, house numbers, zip codes, cities, dates and the German tax ID were found with confidence around 0.99–1.00.
- **Weaknesses:** it's weak on structured PII, as its card says. It caught only the first piece of an email and missed `+31 6 1234 5678` entirely. It tagged a card number as `PHONE` and `user_id 48213` as `ZIP_CODE`.
- **Cost:** `onnxruntime-node` pulls in binaries for every platform, about 300 MB in `node_modules`.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__link_pull_request
tools.description: Link a PR to this thread. T3 shows its status and settles the thread on merge.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__unwatch_pull_request
tools.description: Stop watching a PR for this thread. It stays linked.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__watch_pull_request
tools.description: Watch an open PR for this thread, linking it first if needed. T3 wakes you on failed checks, passed required checks, new comments or reviews, or conflicts. Handle old comments first. Only later ones wake you. After this call, end your turn. The watch stays on after each wake, so do not call this again on a wake. A wake is not a merge decision. Check readiness yourself.

**Complexity: yes.** This touches several subsystems (services, rules, types, tests, package.json). It changes cached data (`cacheSignature`, redactor.ts:258-259). It adds a new native dependency (`onnxruntime-node` is not in `node_modules`). The request has no acceptance criteria, only a trial goal. The label set differs from the native one, which changes behaviour.

### 1. Every touchpoint with `@desert-ant-labs/redact`

- **Imports:** `src/services/redactor.ts:1-2` (`Redact`, `LoadOptions`, `RedactLabel`, and the value import `Redact as NativeRedact`). `src/rules/default-rules.ts:1` (`RedactLabel`). `src/types.ts:1-3` (re-exports `RedactLabel`, `RedactionItem`, `Redaction`; I found no in-repo use of the last two outside this file).

- **Call shape:** `redactor.ts:411-414`: `redactInstance.redaction(source, { labels: pass.labels, minimumConfidence: pass.confidence })`.
- **Result fields consumed** (`passResult.items`, sorted by `start`, `redactor.ts` around 418-446): `item.original` (truthy check), `item.start` and `item.end` (typeof check, with an `indexOf` fallback if the slice does not match), `item.label` (passed to `vault.tokenFor` at 439 and `findRuleForNativeLabel` at 440), `item.confidence` (stored on `RedactionDetail`). **Not consumed:** `redactedText`, `placeholder`, `restore`.
- **Dispose:** `redactor.ts:196-204` (`instance.dispose()`, clears `instance`, `initPromise`, cache). Called from `src/hooks/index.ts:243-244` on `session_shutdown`.
- **Stderr wrapper:** `src/services/native-stderr.ts:37` (koffi import), `:77` (`withSilencedNativeStderr`), `:78` (`PI_PII_REDACT_NATIVE_LOGS` env opt-out). Only call site: `redactor.ts:167`.
- **Config fields:** `modelDirectory` in `src/types.ts:83`, `redactor.ts:161-162` and `:259`. `minimumConfidence` in `src/types.ts:79`, default `redactor.ts:95`, and used at `redactor.ts:259`, `:398`, `:404`, `:413`.
- **Cache key:** `redactor.ts:258-259` (`cacheSignature` = `minimumConfidence|modelDirectory`). `cacheGet` at `:262-272` clears the whole cache when the signature changes. Input text is the key. Cache is also cleared by `setEnabled` (:120), `toggleRule` (:144), `setVault` (:214), `dispose` (:203).
- **Other:** `native-stderr` is the only place `koffi` is used in `src`.

### 2. Two-pass inference and label mapping

- `redactor.ts:49-59` `OPEN_VOCABULARY_LABELS`: GIVEN_NAME, SURNAME, STREET_NAME, CITY, STATE, BUILDING_NUMBER, SECONDARY_ADDRESS, ORG, URL. Every other label is "structured".
- `redactor.ts:380-405`: the structured pass runs only if the text (vault tokens and `[A-Z0-9_]` brackets removed) contains `\d{2,}` (line 394). Its confidence is `min(minimumConfidence, 0.60)` (line 398). The open pass uses `minimumConfidence` (line 404). Default `minimumConfidence` is 0.85 (line 95). - DATE and AGE: not in `RedactLabel` (closed union from the package), so they need a local type, new rule definitions, and a `LABEL_TO_RULE_ID` update.

### 3. How tests get the model

- `vitest.config.ts:7` (30 s timeout), `:8` (`setupFiles: tests/setup-shared-model.ts`), `:11` (`fileParallelism: false`).
- `tests/setup-shared-model.ts:7-22` spies on the native `Redact.load` for every test file, caches one instance per options key, and makes `dispose` a no-op (line 15).

export interface NerDetectOptions { labels: readonly string[]; minimumConfidence: number }

The cleanest approach is minimally invasive: have the masker backend implement the same duck-typed shape as `Redact`, so `redactor.ts` barely changes — it just picks the loader based on an environment flag like `PI_PII_REDACT_BACKEND=masker-mini` inside `getRedactInstance`.

For labels not supported by the masker, I'll just filter them out internally rather than erroring, and since masker-only labels like DATE/AGE won't be requested unless a rule asks for them, this keeps the trial focused on parity across shared labels.

For model acquisition, I'll download from Hugging Face pinned to a specific revision SHA, verify the file hash, and cache it locally under `~/.cache/pi-pii-redact/masker-mini/<sha>/`. For dependencies like onnxruntime-node and the tokenizer library, I'll keep them as devDependencies with a dynamic import and clear error message so published package users aren't affected — this is experimental enough that it doesn't need a changeset yet.

For offset mapping, I'm porting the Swift approach: building a normalized text via per-codepoint NFKC, tracking origin indices back to the original string, then aligning tokenizer output greedily against that normalized text, falling back to null offsets for unalignable tokens (like UNK or byte-fallback pieces) and resyncing at the next token.

For chunking long inputs, I'm using fixed-size windows similar to the Swift CoreML implementation — around 254 content tokens with 32 token overlap — then deduplicating overlapping predictions across windows.

For the session setup, I'm configuring the ONNX inference session with a model variant toggle via env var (int4 vs fp16), and adding caching for the masker model in test setup similar to how the existing Redact model loader is spied on, so tests don't reload the model repeatedly. For evaluation, I plan to run the full suite with the masker-mini backend enabled, write a small comparison script against a labelled corpus, and manually inspect detections on sample texts to validate accuracy before finalizing the task.

Keeping my implementation scope tight: just the backend, wiring, and unit tests for the decoder, aligner, and chunker, while I personally handle the comparison runs. I also need to pull the HF model revision and its sha256 checksums.

- Observed model behaviour: it is "boundary-first" and tags names/addresses/dates/ages well; structured types are weak (an email gets B-EMAIL on its first piece then O; phone numbers may be missed). That's expected; the trial is to measure it. Do not add heuristics to "fix" model output.

## What RedactorService needs (src/services/redactor.ts)
It only consumes: `engine.redaction(text, { labels, minimumConfidence })` -> `{ items: Array<{ label, original, start, end, confidence }> }` and `engine.dispose()`. Loading is in `getRedactInstance()` (lines ~152-188, wraps native load in `withSilencedNativeStderr` + warm-up). The two-pass logic (~376-460) and everything else stays unchanged.

1. Define a minimal local interface (e.g. `NerEngine` in a new file under src/services/) with exactly those consumed members, such that the native `Redact` instance is assignable to it. Retype `instance`, `initPromise`, `RedactorServiceOptions.redactInstance` and `getRedactInstance()` to it.    - `model-files.ts`: pinned revision, file list + hashes, resolve/download/verify.
   - `tokenize.ts`: offset-aware encoding. Approach: build a normalized string by applying NFKC per code point (Array.from(text)) while recording, for each UTF-16 unit of the normalized string, the [start,end) range in the original text; encode the normalized text with the HF tokenizer (without special tokens if the API allows, otherwise strip [CLS]/[SEP]); align each piece (strip leading "▁"; skip empty pieces and special/unk tokens) greedily against the normalized string from a cursor, skipping whitespace; if a piece can't be found at the cursor (after whitespace), give that token a null range and don't advance; map aligned normalized ranges back to original ranges. Return per content token `{ id, range: [start,end] | null }`.
   - `chunk.ts`: windows of max 256 tokens incl. [CLS]/[SEP] (254 content), overlap 32, like Chunker.swift.
   - `decode.ts`: BIOES decode exactly per BIOESDecoder.swift (O or unknown closes a span; I/E continue only same type; S and E close; stray I/E opens; span range = min start..max end of its tokens' ranges, ignoring null ranges; confidence = mean softmax prob of the argmax class over its tokens). Trim whitespace from span edges.

Inference via onnxruntime-node InferenceSession (set session logSeverityLevel to 3 so ORT warnings don't hit stderr / Pi's TUI). Per window: build int64 tensors, run, softmax per token. Merge spans across windows: dedupe overlapping spans (prefer higher confidence, then longer). Filter: keep only labels in `options.labels` and confidence >= minimumConfidence. If `labels` is empty or undefined, return no items (note native treats empty as ALL; redactor never passes empty anyway). `original` = text.slice(start,end). - `src/services/masker-mini/chunk.ts`: 254-token windows with 32 overlap.

- `tests/masker-mini/integration.test.ts`: 13 real-model tests, gated by `describe.runIf(process.env.PI_PII_REDACT_TEST_MASKER)`.

- `src/services/redactor.ts`: `instance`, `initPromise`, `redactInstance` and `getRedactInstance()` are now typed `NerEngine`. The backend env var is read inside `getRedactInstance()`:
  - Unset or `desert-ant` runs the existing code untouched.

  - Any other value throws `Unknown PI_PII_REDACT_BACKEND ...`, and `initPromise` is reset.
  - The constructor seam is unchanged.
- `tests/setup-shared-model.ts`: when `PI_PII_REDACT_BACKEND=masker-mini`, it also shares one `MaskerMini.load` per worker with `dispose` as a no-op. The default branch is untouched.
- `package.json` and `package-lock.json`: `onnxruntime-node` ^1.31.1 and `@huggingface/tokenizers` ^0.2.0 as devDependencies.
- `AGENTS.md`: added the "Experimental: masker-mini backend" note.

## Validation
- `npm run typecheck`: clean.
- `npm test` (default backend): 15 files passed, 1 skipped (the gated integration file). 396 tests passed, 13 skipped.
- `PI_PII_REDACT_TEST_MASKER=1 PI_PII_REDACT_MASKER_DIR=/tmp/mm-spike/model npx vitest run tests/masker-mini`: 45 of 45 passed.

**Full-suite failures on masker-mini**
Every one of these fails because the model misses or mislabels credit cards and phones, apart from the dispose test.
1. `tier1 4.2 US dot-separated phone`: expected undefined to be 'transform'. The phone was not detected.
2. `tier1 5.1 hyphen-separated credit card`: same assertion. No detection.
3. `tier1 5.2 space-separated credit card`: same assertion. No detection.
4. `tier1 5.4 Visa format`: output was "Visa test card: [PHONE_1#..]". It was labelled PHONE, not CREDIT_CARD.
5. `tier1 5.5 Mastercard format`: output was "[GOVERNMENT_ID_1][PHONE_1][GOVERNMENT_ID_2]". The card was split and mislabelled.
6. `tier2 2.4 repeated identical phones`: expected undefined to be 'transform'. No detection.
7. `tier2 2.5 repeated identical credit cards`: expected undefined to be 2. No detection.
8. `tier2 4.5 credit card among math/currency symbols`: no detection.
9. `tier3 3.1 five PII types in one prompt`: the credit card `4532-1234-5678-9012` is left in plaintext.
10. `tier4 4.5 JSON customer profile`: the credit card is left in plaintext.
11. `stress-challenger "handles re-initialization cleanly after dispose()"`: expected +0 to be 2. This is a harness artifact. The shared instance's `dispose` is a no-op and the test counts native-instance load calls.

## Notes
- **Alignment deviation (lookahead resync):** after an `[UNK]` token (emoji, since there is no byte fallback), the next piece may be found up to 32 UTF-16 units ahead. Without this, one emoji nulled every later token in the text. An integration test covers it.
- **Alignment deviation (skipped characters):** the alignment cursor also skips control and format characters, not only whitespace. The tokenizer's normalizer drops them.
- **NFKC grouping:** NFKC is applied per cluster (a code point plus its following combining marks), not per bare code point. Per code point would break "e" + U+0301.
- **Filter order:** I filter by label and confidence first, then dedupe overlapping windows. This stops an unwanted label from suppressing a wanted one.
- **User directory:** a `PI_PII_REDACT_MASKER_DIR` directory is verified but never modified or deleted. The cache path deletes corrupt files and re-downloads.
- **ORT telemetry:** `onnxruntime-node` writes a `Microsoft/DeveloperTools/.onnxruntime` database under `XDG_CACHE_HOME`. That is ORT behaviour, not ours.
- **Install script:** npm warned that the `onnxruntime-node` postinstall is not approved. The binaries were already present under `bin/napi-v6`, so nothing was needed.

All tests passed (396 default-backend tests, 13 skipped, plus masker tests for both variants), but the e2e tiers miss names and developer-text false positives, so I'll build a side-by-side benchmark running the same corpus through `RedactorService` for each backend.
