90:| Secrets | `secrets`: provider API keys, tokens, JWTs, private keys, credentials in connection URLs (see [Secret detection](#secret-detection)) | secret scanner |
91-|  | `api-key-generic`: `sk-…`, GitHub `ghp_…`, GitLab `glpat-…`, AWS `AKIA…` (fallback if the scanner is unavailable) | rules |
92-| Dates | `date` (**disabled by default**: dates in logs and changelogs are noisy; enable it with `/pii toggle date`) | model |
93-
94-`REDACTEDport`, `drivers-license` and `tax-id` are aliases of `government-id`, so toggling them toggles that rule. The `state`, `secondary-address`, `url` and `org` rules were removed because no detector backs them any more.
95-
96:## Secret detection
97-
98-The `secrets` rule ("Secrets & credentials", on by default) uses [`@visulima/secret-scanner`](https://github.com/visulima/secret-scanner), a Rust port of the gitleaks rule set (plus kingfisher rules, about 1000 rules). It finds API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, AWS, Hugging Face, Slack, SendGrid, Google, GitLab and GitHub, JWTs, PEM private keys, credentials in URLs such as `REDACTED`, and `REDACTEDword = "..."` style assignments. Matches become `[SECRET_n#xxxx]` tokens that are restored in tool-call arguments and assistant replies like any other token.
99-
100-- Offline only: the scanner runs locally and its credential validation (which would send secrets to provider APIs or connect to databases) is hard-coded off.
101-- Cost: every scanner call has a fixed cost of about 24 ms. A cheap pre-check (long token-like runs, PEM headers, URL credentials, `REDACTEDword=`/`token:` style assignments) skips the call for text that cannot contain a secret.
102-- Noise control: matches shorter than 8 characters and matches containing whitespace (except private keys) are dropped.
103-- Known gaps: `npm_` tokens and the AWS documentation example key are not detected by the scanner.
104-- Toggle it with `/pii toggle secrets` (aliases `secret`, `credentials`). `/pii status` shows whether the scanner loaded. If its native binding is unavailable on your platform, secret detection is skipped and the regex-based `api-key-generic` rule still applies; all PII detection keeps working.
105-- Requires Node `^22.14.0 || >=24.10.0`.
106-
107-## The model
108-

"@chrisdoc/pi-pii-redact": minor

Add secret and credential detection using `@visulima/secret-scanner`. A new `secrets` rule (on by default, toggle with `/pii toggle secrets`) replaces API keys, tokens, JWTs, private keys and credentials in URLs with `[SECRET_n#xxxx]` tokens that are restored like other tokens. Detection runs offline (credential validation is hard-coded off) behind a regex pre-gate, and falls back to the existing regex rules if the native binding cannot load. `/pii status` shows the scanner state. Matches become `[SECRET_n#xxxx]` tokens that are restored in tool-call arguments and assistant replies like any other token.

+The `secrets` rule ("Secrets & credentials", on by default) uses [`@visulima/secret-scanner`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@visulima/secret-scanner), a Rust port of gitleaks-style detection. It runs the bundled kingfisher rules (about 870) plus a few gitleaks rules (GitHub, Hugging Face, npm); the rest of the gitleaks set is left out because it would add about 500 MB of memory and several seconds of start-up for little extra coverage. It finds API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, AWS, Hugging Face, Slack, SendGrid, Google, GitLab and GitHub, JWTs, PEM private keys, credentials in URLs such as `REDACTED`, and `REDACTEDword = "..."` style assignments. Matches become `[SECRET_n#xxxx]` tokens that are restored in tool-call arguments and assistant replies like any other token.
- Offline only: the scanner runs locally and its credential validation (which would send secrets to provider APIs or connect to databases) is hard-coded off.

-- Cost: every scanner call has a fixed cost of about 24 ms. A cheap pre-check (long token-like runs, PEM headers, URL credentials, `password=`/`token:` style assignments) skips the call for text that cannot contain a secret.

+- Cost: about 170 MB of memory and a ~0.8 s warm-up, started in the background when a session starts. After that every scanner call has a fixed cost of about 25 ms; a cheap pre-check (long token-like runs, PEM headers, URL credentials, `password=`/`token:` style assignments) skips the call for text that cannot contain a secret.
- Noise control: matches shorter than 8 characters and matches containing whitespace (except private keys) are dropped.
- Known gaps: `npm_` tokens and the AWS documentation example key are not detected by the scanner.

- Toggle it with `/pii toggle secrets` (aliases `secret`, `credentials`). `/pii status` shows whether the scanner loaded. If its native binding is unavailable on your platform, secret detection is skipped and the regex-based `api-key-generic` rule still applies; all PII detection keeps working.
4. Applies the regex overlays. `replaceOutsideTokens` never touches text overlapping an existing vault token.
5. Runs ONE model call for all active model labels, filtered by `minimumConfidence` (default 0.55). No call is made when no model label is active.

-**Secret scanner (`src/services/secrets/`)** wraps `@visulima/secret-scanner` (native, loaded lazily with dynamic import; a load failure only marks it `unavailable`, see `getSecretScannerStatus()`). Never enable its `validate` option (it would send secrets to provider APIs) and never write to stdout/stderr from it (Pi's TUI). A regex pre-gate skips the ~24 ms per-call cost for text that cannot hold a secret. Findings are mapped to offsets by searching for `finding.secret` near the reported line/column, then filtered (min length 8, no whitespace except private keys); overlaps resolve by confidence, then narrowest. Tests must generate realistic provider keys at runtime (`tests/secrets/fake-keys.ts`) because GitHub push protection rejects committed ones.

Commit subject: "feat: detect secrets and credentials with @visulima/secret-scanner"
PR title: same.
PR body facts:
Summary: adds a `secrets` rule (on by default) backed by @visulima/secret-scanner (MIT, Rust/N-API port of gitleaks-style detection). Detected keys become `[SECRET_n#xxxx]` tokens, restored in tool-call args and replies like other tokens, so the agent can use credentials without seeing them. Stacked on #18.
Changes:
- New src/services/secrets/: lazy native load (failure => status "unavailable", PII detection unaffected, regex `api-key-generic` fallback stays), regex pre-gate, line/column -> UTF-16 offset mapping, span filtering (min 8 chars, no whitespace except private keys), overlap resolution (higher confidence, then narrowest), widening of partial key spans to the whole token.
- Runs after the vault fast path and before regex overlays/model, so phone/IBAN/email rules can't grab parts of a key.
- Offline only: scanner validation (which would send secrets to providers / connect to DBs) is hard-coded off; test asserts it on every call.
- Ruleset trimmed to the kingfisher rules + a few gitleaks rules (GitHub, Hugging Face, npm): full bundled set costs ~660 MB RSS and ~4 s first-scan; trimmed ~170 MB and ~0.8 s, warmed in the background at session_start. ~25 ms per scan after that, skipped by the pre-gate for most text.
- `/pii status` shows scanner state; aliases `secret`, `credentials`.
- engines.node is now `^22.14.0 || >=24.10.0` (scanner requirement).
- Clean-exit child-process test now also loads the scanner and asserts empty stdout/stderr.
- Test changes: e2e harness and hooks token regexes accept SECRET; rule count 19 -> 20; tier4 4.3 asserts the IP is gone (it's now inside the SECRET token of the postgres URL) instead of an IP placeholder.
Eval (370-case corpus): API_KEY recall 5/6 -> 6/6, `secrets` false positives 0, no-pii FPs unchanged (45 in 33/125), median latency 14.2 ms (unchanged), peak RSS 458 MB (eval process).
Known gaps: npm_ tokens not detected by the scanner; AWS documentation example key only caught by the regex fallback.
Verification: `npm run typecheck` clean; `npm test` 22 files / 654 tests pass locally (aarch64, Node 24); eval as above.

Return the PR URL and head SHA.

# AGENTS.md

This file provides guidance to coding agents working with code in this repository.

## What this is

A [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) extension (published as `@chrisdoc/pi-pii-redact`) that replaces PII and secrets with stable per-session tokens like `[EMAIL_3#k7q2]` before anything reaches the LLM, and restores real values in tool-call arguments and assistant replies. Detection runs locally: the masker-mini NER model (ONNX Runtime) plus deterministic, validator-backed regex overlay rules.

The package ships TypeScript source directly (`main` and `pi.extensions` point at `src/index.ts`); there is no build step.

## Commands

```bash
npm install
npm run typecheck                         # tsc --noEmit (covers src/ only)
npm test                                  # vitest run, all suites
npx vitest run tests/vault.test.ts        # one file
npx vitest run tests/e2e                  # e2e tiers only
npx vitest run -t "restores tokens"       # tests matching a name
pi -e .                                   # load the working copy into Pi
```

Most tests run the real on-device model on CPU. `tests/setup-shared-model.ts` loads it once per test file and shares it across services (`dispose()` is a no-op there), so tests that assert model-disposal behavior see the shared instance. On first run it downloads the pinned model (~22 MB) into `~/.cache/pi-pii-redact` (or set `PI_PII_REDACT_MODEL_DIR` to use a local copy). `vitest.config.ts` sets a 30 s timeout and `fileParallelism: false` on purpose, because parallel files each load a model and oversubscribe the CPU. Don't change those to speed things up.

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs typecheck and tests on Node 22 and 24.

## Architecture

`src/index.ts` creates one `RedactorService` and one `PiiStats` and passes both to `registerHooks` (`src/hooks/index.ts`) and `registerPiiCommands` (`src/commands/pii.ts`).

**`RedactorService` (`src/services/redactor.ts`)** owns the rules, the config, the lazily loaded masker-mini model, an LRU result cache and the session vault. `redact()` runs in this order:
1. Splits enabled rules into regex overlay rules (those with a `pattern`), the secret-scanner rule (`detector: "secret-scanner"`, never sent to the model) and model labels.
2. Fast path: replaces originals already in the vault with their tokens.
3. Secrets: `scanSecrets` (`src/services/secrets/`) replaces keys/tokens/private keys with `[SECRET_n#...]` tokens, before the overlays so a key wins over phone/IBAN/email rules.
4. Applies the regex overlays. `replaceOutsideTokens` never touches text overlapping an existing vault token.
5. Runs ONE model call for all active model labels, filtered by `minimumConfidence` (default 0.55). No call is made when no model label is active.

**Secret scanner (`src/services/secrets/`)** wraps `@visulima/secret-scanner` (native, loaded lazily with dynamic import; a load failure only marks it `unavailable`, see `getSecretScannerStatus()`). Never enable its `validate` option (it would send secrets to provider APIs) and never write to stdout/stderr from it (Pi's TUI). The gitleaks keyword-context rules are filtered out (`trimRuleset`; the full bundled set costs ~660 MB and ~4 s cold start, trimmed ~200 MB and ~1.3 s); the first scan is paid once during load and warmed at `session_start`. A regex pre-gate skips the ~25 ms per-call cost for text that cannot hold a secret. Spans that cover only part of a key-like token are widened to the whole token. Findings are mapped to offsets by searching for `finding.secret` near the reported line/column, then filtered (min length 8, no whitespace except private keys); overlaps resolve by confidence, then narrowest. Tests must generate realistic provider keys at runtime (`tests/secrets/fake-keys.ts`) because GitHub push protection rejects committed ones.

Anything that changes rules, the enabled state or the vault must clear the cache, as the existing setters do.

**`PiiVault` (`src/services/vault.ts`)** is the two-way map between originals and tokens. The same original always gets the same token. Per-label counters only increase. A random per-vault nonce means text that merely looks like a token is never restored. Restore tolerates mangled tokens (lower case, missing brackets, extra spaces). Rules with a custom `mask` are one-way and never enter the vault.

**Rules (`src/rules/default-rules.ts`)**: `MODEL_RULE_DEFINITIONS` holds the model-backed rules (given-name, surname, street-name, building-number, city, zip-code, government-id, age, and `date`, which is disabled by default) and the deterministic overlays with `validate` functions from `src/rules/validators.ts` (email, bank-account/IBAN, imei, credit-card, ssn, routing-number, ip-address, phone). `DETERMINISTIC_RULES` adds `nl-bsn`; `SECRET_RULES` adds API keys. The model's EMAIL/PHONE/CREDIT_CARD labels are never requested. `passport`, `drivers-license` and `tax-id` are aliases of `government-id`. `toggleRule` accepts ids, labels and aliases.

**Model engine (`src/services/masker-mini/`)**: `MaskerMini` implements the minimal `NerEngine` interface (`src/services/ner-engine.ts`, which also defines `NerLabel`); tests inject fakes through `RedactorServiceOptions.redactInstance`. `model-files.ts` pins the Hugging Face revision and SHA-256 of the int4 files, downloads into `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/pi-pii-redact/masker-mini/<rev>/` (default `~/.cache`), or uses `RedactorConfig.modelDirectory` / `PI_PII_REDACT_MODEL_DIR` (hashes still verified, never downloads). `tokenize.ts` aligns tokens to original offsets, `chunk.ts` windows long texts, `decode.ts` does BIOES decoding, `postprocess.ts` cleans spans (edge punctuation, numeric spans glued into identifiers, partial-word names), `merge.ts` filters and de-duplicates. `onnxruntime-node` and `@huggingface/tokenizers` are loaded with a dynamic import; `ORT_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` is set right before it (ORT's Linux telemetry writes under `~/.cache/Microsoft`), and `tests/masker-mini/telemetry.test.ts` checks that in a child process. Source must stay Node strip-only TypeScript compatible (no enums, namespaces or parameter properties). `eval/` holds a labelled corpus and scorer (see `eval/README.md`).

**Hooks (`src/hooks/index.ts`)** handle the Pi events:
- Redaction: `input`, `tool_result` (including `structuredContent`) and `context`. `context` re-redacts the whole history before every provider request.
- Restore: `tool_call` restores arguments in place, and `message_end` restores the assistant reply. Both run even while redaction is off, as long as the vault has entries.
- `session_before_compact` / `session_before_tree`: these call the model directly and bypass `context`, so the extension runs `compact` / `generateBranchSummary` itself on redacted input. **On any failure they return `{ cancel: true }`** and never fall back to plaintext.
- `session_start` rebuilds the vault and config from session entries. `session_shutdown` disposes the model.

**Message walkers (`src/hooks/messages.ts`)** deep-map strings through messages and content blocks. Invariants: never mutate the input, return the *same reference* when nothing changed (hooks use reference equality to decide whether to return a result), and leave assistant `thinking` blocks byte-identical because providers sign them.

**Usage stats (`src/services/stats.ts`, `src/commands/stats-board.ts`)**: `PiiStats` holds in-memory counters for the current run, recorded by the hooks. `context` re-masking is counted separately and never added to totals, because it re-redacts the whole history each turn. `/pii stats` combines them with per-label counts from the vault and renders a board (a scrollable overlay in TUI mode, plain `notify` text otherwise). It shows counts only, never originals or tokens.

**Persistence (`src/hooks/persist.ts`)**: state lives in session custom entries. `pii-vault` entries are append-only deltas from `vault.takePendingDelta()`. Call `persistVaultDelta` after any redaction that may have minted tokens. The vault is rebuilt from *all* entries across branches so numbers are never reused. `pii-config` holds the latest enabled state plus disabled rule ids. Session files therefore contain plaintext originals by design; the extension protects what reaches the model, not what is on disk.

## Tests

- `tests/mock-pi.ts` provides `createMockExtensionAPI` (captures handlers and `appendEntry` as session entries), `createMockContext` and `createMockRedactor` (no model) for unit tests.
- `tests/e2e/harness.ts` provides `PiTestHarness` for opaque-box tests through the public entry points, plus `assertRedacted*` matchers. The tiers cover features, boundaries, combinations, workflows and adversarial cases (`tier1` to `tier5`). The core assertion is that the original value is absent from the output and a placeholder is present.
- `TEST_INFRA.md` / `TEST_READY.md` describe the e2e methodology. They reference `ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md` / `PROJECT.md`, which are not in the repo.

## Releasing

Use Changesets. Any PR that changes behavior needs a changeset (`npx changeset`, committed in `.changeset/`). Merging to `main` opens a "Version Packages" PR, and merging that publishes to npm via OIDC trusted publishing and creates a GitHub release (`.github/workflows/publish.yml`). Don't hand-edit the `version` in `package.json` or `CHANGELOG.md`.

## claude.ai executor
# Executor

## What Executor is

Executor is a host that runs apps: TypeScript packages that expose tools,
storage, UI, accounts and background work. Agents reach every app through the
MCP tools `skills`, `search`, `describe`, `call` and `execute`, with each app's
slug as its namespace. Credentials go only through Executor's secure connection
links, never through chat or source code. Some calls pause for user approval.

This is the Executor app's `executor` skill. Read its other skills with
`skills({app: "executor", name: "code-mode"})`; `skills({})` lists them all.

## Find and call tools

`search({ query: "..." })` returns each tool's exact `path`, such as
`tools.<slug>.<tool>`, and input type; `describe({ paths })` returns full
signatures. Never guess argument names.

For a few independent calls, use `call({ calls: { path, input } })`; an array
of calls runs concurrently. Each result has `ok` and its `value` or `error`.

Write a JavaScript program for `execute` when one call's result feeds another,
or a large result should be filtered before it reaches you. Inside it, the same
paths are async functions, and `tools.search` and `tools.search.describe` work
as above. Return only the data you need. For depth, read the `code-mode` skill.
When `call` or `execute` pauses for approval or input, show the request to the
user and resume it; never repeat the call or run the program again.

## Build an app

Build an app when no existing app provides the tools, data, UI or automation
the user needs. For a known service, search the catalog first:
`organization.catalog({ query: { search: "gmail", limit: "20" } })`, then
`apps.install` a match or `apps.importCustom` a remote MCP URL. With a shell,
use the `executor apps` CLI, else `execute`; read the `app-authoring` skill first.

## Send feedback

Send feedback with the Executor app's `feedback.submit` tool when Executor gets
in your way, can't do something you need, works especially well, or the user
has feedback. Before your final reply, check whether anything is worth
reporting. Be specific; never include credentials or user data (`feedback.md`).

# Executor

## What Executor is

Executor is a host that runs apps: TypeScript packages that expose tools,
storage, UI, accounts and background work. Agents reach every app through the
MCP tools `skills`, `search`, `describe`, `call` and `execute`, with each app's
slug as its namespace. Credentials go only through Executor's secure connection
links, never through chat or source code. Some calls pause for user approval.

This is the Executor app's `executor` skill. Read its other skills with
`skills({app: "executor", name: "code-mode"})`; `skills({})` lists them all.

## Find and call tools

`search({ query: "..." })` returns each tool's exact `path`, such as
`tools.<slug>.<tool>`, and input type; `describe({ paths })` returns full
signatures. Never guess argument names.

For a few independent calls, use `call({ calls: { path, input } })`; an array
of calls runs concurrently. Each result has `ok` and its `value` or `error`.

Write a JavaScript program for `execute` when one call's result feeds another,
or a large result should be filtered before it reaches you. Inside it, the same
paths are async functions, and `tools.search` and `tools.search.describe` work
as above. Return only the data you need. For depth, read the `code-mode` skill.
When `call` or `execute` pauses for approval or input, show the request to the
user and resume it; never repeat the call or run the program again.

## Build an app

Build an app when no existing app provides the tools, data, UI or automation
the user needs. For a known service, search the catalog first:
`organization.catalog({ query: { search: "gmail", limit: "20" } })`, then
`apps.install` a match or `apps.importCustom` a remote MCP URL. With a shell,
use the `executor apps` CLI, else `execute`; read the `app-authoring` skill first.

## Send feedback

Send feedback with the Executor app's `feedback.submit` tool when Executor gets
in your way, can't do something you need, works especially well, or the user
has feedback. Before your final reply, check whether anything is worth
reporting. Be specific; never include credentials or user data (`feedback.md`).
